Household Expenditure and Podcast Performance: Regression Analysis in R

Part 1: Household Expenditure in England

This dataset contains weekly expenditure information for households in England, with each row representing one household. The primary outcome of interest is weekly food expenditure (£). Explanatory variables include household composition, respondent characteristics, and weekly spending on housing, alcohol, and non-mortgage debt repayments.

The analysis examines how these factors relate to food expenditure, with particular focus on alcohol spending and whether its association with food expenditure differs across households with different levels of debt.

The table below provides a brief description of each variable in the data set

Data Dictionary

Variable Description
Kids Total Number of children in the household
Household Size Total number of individuals residing in the household
Sex Gender of the survey respondent
Vehicles Total Number of vehicles in the household
Food Average weekly household expenditure on food,measured in pounds (£)
Housing Average weekly household housing costs,including rent or mortgage payments, measured in pounds (£)
Alcohol Average weekly household expenditure on alcoholic beverages, measured in pounds (£)
Debt Average weekly household repayments on non-mortgage debt, measured in pounds (£)
Income_category Categorical indicator of household income level: Low, Medium, or High

Data overview

Overall, the data appear suitable for modelling, with no clear evidence of abnormal values or implausible outliers after handling a small amount of missing data

Handling Inconsistency in data

To ensure consistency and comparability across analyses, only households with complete information on all relevant variables were retained. Moreover, Categorical variables were converted to factors prior to modelling

#filtering out missing data
Filtered_data <- household %>%
  filter(
    !is.na(Kids),
    !is.na(HouseholdSize),
    !is.na(Sex),
    !is.na(Vehicles),
    !is.na(Food),
    !is.na(Housing),
    !is.na(Alcohol),
    !is.na(Debt),
    !is.na(income_category))
# Converting categorical variables to factors
Filtered_data <- Filtered_data %>% mutate(income_category = factor(income_category,levels=c("Low","Medium","High")),Sex = factor(Sex))

Visualizing distributions of variables of interest

Food Distribution

ggplot(Filtered_data, aes(Food)) +
geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "lightblue", colour = "black") +
geom_vline(aes(xintercept = mean(Food)), colour = "red") +
theme_minimal() +
labs(title = "Distribution of Weekly Food Expenditure",
x = "Weekly Food Spend (£)", y = "Number of Households")

Interpretation

Weekly food expenditure is broadly centred around typical values with a mild right tail. The pattern appears plausible for household spending data, with no obvious anomalies that would prevent linear modelling

Alcohal Distribution

ggplot(Filtered_data, aes(Alcohol)) +
geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "lightblue", colour = "black") +
geom_vline(aes(xintercept = mean(Alcohol)), colour = "red") +
theme_minimal() +
labs(title = "Distribution of Weekly Alcohol Expenditure",
x = "Weekly Alcohol Spend (£)", y = "Number of Households")

Interpretation

Alcohol expenditure is concentrated around modest weekly amounts with mild skew. The distribution looks plausible and suitable for use as a continuous predictor

Debt Payments Distribution

ggplot(Filtered_data, aes(Debt)) +
geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "lightblue", colour = "black") +
geom_vline(aes(xintercept = mean(Debt)), colour = "red") +
theme_minimal() +
labs(title = "Distribution of Weekly Debt Payments",
x = "Weekly Debt Payments (£)", y = "Number of Households")

Interpretation

Debt repayments vary widely, with many households clustered at lower repayment levels and fewer households at higher values. This pattern is consistent with meaningful differences in financial obligations rather than data error

Visualizing Relationships of variables of interest

Food vs Alcohol

ggplot(Filtered_data, aes(x = Alcohol, y = Food, colour = income_category)) +
geom_point(alpha = 0.25) +
geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
theme_minimal() +
labs(title = "Food vs Alcohol by Income Category",
x = "Weekly Alcohol Spend (£)", y = "Weekly Food Spend (£)",
colour = "Income category")

Interpretation

Visual inspection suggests a positive association between alcohol expenditure and food expenditure. Households that spend more on alcohol also tend to spend more on food. The fitted line indicates a broadly increasing trend, although substantial variability remains. Patterns appear broadly similar across income groups

Food vs Debt

ggplot(Filtered_data, aes(x = Debt, y = Food)) +
geom_point(alpha = 0.2, colour = "lightblue") +
geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, colour = "darkblue") +
theme_minimal() +
labs(title = "Food vs Debt Payments",
x = "Weekly Debt Payments (£)", y = "Weekly Food Spend (£)")

Interpretation

Visual inspection suggests a weak negative association between debt repayments and food expenditure. While the fitted line indicates a slightly decreasing trend, the scatter remains substantial, suggesting debt alone explains limited variation in food spending

Food vs Housing.

ggplot(Filtered_data, aes(x = Housing, y = Food)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.2, colour = "lightblue") +
geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, colour = "darkblue") +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "Food Expenditure vs Housing Costs",
    x = "Weekly Housing Costs (£)",
    y = "Weekly Food Expenditure (£)")

Interpretation

Visual inspection suggests a clear positive association between housing costs and food expenditure. Households with higher housing costs also tend to spend more on food, and the fitted line indicates a broadly increasing trend

Food vs Alcohol across debt bands

Filtered_data %>%
mutate(DebtBand = cut(
Debt,
breaks = quantile(Debt, probs = c(0, .33, .66, 1), na.rm = TRUE),
include.lowest = TRUE,
labels = c("Low debt", "Medium debt", "High debt")
)) %>%
ggplot(aes(x = Alcohol, y = Food)) +
geom_point(alpha = 0.2, colour = "lightblue") +
geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, colour = "darkblue") +
facet_wrap(~ DebtBand) +
theme_minimal() +
labs(title = "Food vs Alcohol Across Debt Bands",
x = "Weekly Alcohol Spend (£)", y = "Weekly Food Spend (£)")

Interpretation

The fitted lines appear broadly similar across low, medium, and high-debt groups. There is no clear visual evidence that the alcohol–food relationship differs by debt level, motivating formal interaction testing

Together, all these distributions appear realistic and appropriate for linear modelling

Model 1 (Main Effects)

A multiple linear regression model was fitted to examine whether household characteristics and expenditure variables explain variation in weekly food expenditure

Food_Lm <- lm(
Food ~ HouseholdSize + Kids + Vehicles + Housing + income_category + Sex + Alcohol + Debt, data = Filtered_data)

summary(Food_Lm)

Interpretation

NHST: Overall Model Test

H₀: None of the predictors explain Food spending

H₁: At least one predictor affects Food spending.

The overall model was statistically significant, F(9, 4073) = 82.10, p < .001, providing strong evidence against the null hypothesis that none of the predictors are associated with food expenditure.

Model Fit

The model explained 15.4% of the variation in weekly food expenditure (R² = 0.154, adjusted R² = 0.152),indicating a moderate fit for cross sectional household expenditure data.

Key Estimates (Estimation Approach)

Housing expenditure was the strongest predictor. Holding other variables constant, each additional £1 per week spent on housing was associated with an estimated £0.09 increase in food expenditure (β = 0.091, 95% CI [0.085, 0.098], p < .001).

Alcohol expenditure was positively associated with food spending.Each additional £1 spent on alcohol was associated with an estimated £0.39 increase in food expenditure (β = 0.388, 95% CI [0.266, 0.511], p < .001).

Debt repayments were negatively associated with food expenditure. Each additional £1 per week in debt repayments was associated with an estimated £0.05 decrease in food expenditure (β = −0.049, 95% CI [−0.068, −0.030], p < .001).

Non-Significant Predictors

Household size, number of children, number of vehicles, income category, and respondent sex were not statistically significant while housing, alcohol, and debt expenditures were included in the model.

Conclusion

Overall, food expenditure is more strongly related to other financial commitments particularly housing costs, alcohol spending and debt repayments rather than the household demographic characteristics. Although the model is statistically significant, a large proportion of variation in food expenditure remains unexplained

Model 2 (Interaction: Does Debt change Alcohol’s effect?)

A multiple linear regression model was fitted to examine whether household characteristics and expenditure variables explain variation in weekly food expenditure

Food_Lm_Int <- lm(
Food ~ HouseholdSize + Kids + Vehicles + Housing +
income_category + Sex + Alcohol * Debt,
data = Filtered_data
)

The interaction model remained statistically significant, F(10, 4072) = 73.90, p < .001,with virtually identical explanatory power to the main-effects model (R² = 0.154, adjusted R² = 0.152)

Interaction Term (Estimation + NHST)

The Alcohol × Debt interaction was not statistically significant(β = −0.00155, 95% CI [−0.00765, 0.00455], p = .619).This indicates no evidence that debt moderates the association between alcohol expenditure and food expenditure

Anova Test

An ANOVA was used to assess whether adding an Alcohol × Debt interaction improves model fit compared with the main-effects model

anova(Food_Lm, Food_Lm_Int)
Analysis of Variance Table

Model 1: Food ~ HouseholdSize + Kids + Vehicles + Housing + income_category +

1   4073 578186

Interpretation

An ANOVA comparison between the main-effects model and the interaction model confirmed that including the interaction did not improve model fit, F(1, 4072) = 0.25, p = .619.

Conclusion

There is no evidence that the relationship between alcohol expenditure and food expenditure varies across households with different levels of debt. The effect of alcohol spending on food expenditure appears broadly similar regardless of debt repayment levels.

Interpretation

Across all debt levels, predicted food expenditure increases as alcohol spending increases. However, predicted values at the same alcohol level are very similar across low, median, and high debt households. This is consistent with the non-significant Alcohol × Debt interaction and reinforces the conclusion that debt does not meaningfully modify the alcohol-food relationship

Checking Diagnostic of model

Model diagnostics were examined to assess whether the assumptions of linear regression were reasonably satisfied

par(mfrow=c(2,2), mar=c(4,4,2,1))
plot(Food_Lm)

par(mfrow=c(2,2), mar=c(4,4,2,1))
plot(Food_Lm_Int)

par(mfrow=c(1,1))

Interpretation

Diagnostics: Food_Lm (Main-effects model)

Diagnostic plots indicated no major violations of linear regression assumptions. Residuals were approximately normally distributed, with no strong evidence of heteroscedasticity or influential observations, supporting the validity of model inference

Diagnostics: Food_Lm_Int (Alcohol × Debt interaction)

Diagnostic plots for the interaction model were similar to those of the main-effects model. Assumptions of linearity, normality, and constant variance appeared reasonable, indicating that the interaction results can be interpreted reliably

Final Conclusion

Household food expenditure is only partially explained by the variables available in this dataset (R² ≈ 0.15). Housing expenditure and alcohol spending were positively associated with food expenditure, while higher debt repayments were associated with slightly lower food spending. Household demographic characteristics such as household size, number of children, income category, and respondent sex did not show strong independent associations once expenditure variables were included. There was no evidence that household debt modifies the relationship between alcohol and food expenditure, as the Alcohol × Debt interaction was not statistically significant. Overall, food expenditure appears more strongly related to other financial commitments than to household demographics

Part 2: Podcast Streaming Performance

This dataset contains aggregated averages for individual podcasts collected over an extended period, with each row representing a single podcast. The main outcome of interest is average daily listens. Alongside listens, the data record average review score, total number of reviews, subscriber count, and podcast genre.

The analysis explores the relationships between podcast characteristics and listening patterns, with particular focus on review metrics and how their association with daily listens varies across different podcast genres and subscriber levels.

The table below provides a brief description of each variable in the data set

Data Dictionary

Variable Description
Platform Digital platform on which the podcast is hosted
Genre Primary content genre of the podcast
Review.score Primary content genre of the podcast
Daily.listens Average listener review score over the observed period
Total.reviews Total number of listener reviews received over the observed period
Subscribers Total number of subscribers to the podcast at the end of the observed period

Data overview

# Read podcast data

podcasts <- read_csv("podcast_listens.csv", col_names = c( "platform","genre","review.score", "daily.listens", "total.reviews", "subscribers"), skip = 1)

Overall, the data is suitable for modelling and the only clear inconsistency is the number of invalid negative value and outliers in some variable, which are handled in the cleaning step below

Handling inconsistency

The dataset contains 5,400 podcasts and six variables. Inspection revealed a small number of invalid values, including negative subscriber counts (i.e −2) and review scores outside the plausible 1–5 rating scale. Negative subscriber counts are not meaningful in practice, and review scores outside this range are inconsistent with standard podcast rating systems and were rare in the data. These values were therefore treated as data errors and set to missing. A complete-case dataset was then created for the variables used in modelling, resulting in a final analysis sample of n = 5,353 podcasts.

podcasts_filtered <- podcasts %>%
  mutate(
    subscribers   = ifelse(subscribers < 0, NA, subscribers),
    daily.listens = ifelse(daily.listens < 0, NA, daily.listens),
    total.reviews = ifelse(total.reviews < 0, NA, total.reviews),
    review.score  = ifelse(review.score < 0, NA, review.score)
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    review.score = ifelse(review.score < 1 | review.score > 5, NA, review.score),
    platform = factor(platform),
    genre    = factor(genre)
  ) %>%
  filter(
    !is.na(daily.listens),
    !is.na(review.score),
    !is.na(total.reviews),
    !is.na(subscribers),
    !is.na(genre))

  geom_vline(
    xintercept = mean(podcasts_filtered$daily.listens, na.rm = TRUE),
    colour = "red") + theme_minimal() + labs( title = "Distribution of Average Daily Listens", x = "Average Daily Listens",y = "Number of Podcasts")

Interpretation

Daily listens are unimodal with a moderate right tail, indicating that while most podcasts receive similar average listening levels, a smaller number attract substantially larger audiences. Values appear plausible for aggregated listening data and suitable for linear modelling

Review score

ggplot(podcasts_filtered, aes(review.score)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20, fill = "lightblue", colour = "black") +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = mean(review.score)), colour = "red") +
  theme_minimal() + labs(title = "Distribution of Average Review Scores", x = "Average Review Score", y = "Number of Podcasts")

Interpretation

After removing invalid values, review scores are tightly concentrated between 4 and 5, with limited dispersion. This restricted range suggests that while review score may be statistically detectable, it is unlikely to explain large differences in daily listens

Total Number of reviews

ggplot(podcasts_filtered, aes(total.reviews)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "lightblue", colour = "black") +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = mean(total.reviews)), colour = "red") +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Total Reviews",
    x = "Total Number of Reviews",
    y = "Number of Podcasts")

Interpretation

Total reviews are right-skewed, with many podcasts receiving relatively few reviews and a small number receiving very high counts. This pattern is typical of popularity related variables and supports its inclusion as a continuous predictor

Subscribers

ggplot(podcasts_filtered, aes(subscribers)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "lightblue", colour = "black") +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = mean(subscribers)), colour = "red") +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Subscribers",
    x = "Number of Subscribers",
    y = "Number of Podcasts")

Interpretation

Subscriber counts are right-skewed, with most podcasts having modest subscriber bases and a small number having very large audiences. This supports subscribers as a plausible major driver of variation in daily listens

Visualising relationships of Variables of interest

Daily listens vs review score (by genre)

ggplot(podcasts_filtered, aes(x = review.score, y = daily.listens, colour = genre)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "Daily Listens vs Review Score by Genre",
    x = "Average Review Score",
    y = "Average Daily Listens",
    colour = "Genre")

Interpretation

The fitted lines suggest at most a weak positive association between review score and daily listens, with substantial scatter. In contrast, clear baseline differences in listening levels across genres are visible, motivating the inclusion of genre in subsequent regression models

Daily listens vs total reviews

ggplot(podcasts_filtered, aes(x = total.reviews, y = daily.listens)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3, colour = "lightblue") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, colour = "darkblue") +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "Daily Listens vs Total Reviews",
    x = "Total Number of Reviews",
    y = "Average Daily Listens")

Interpretation

A positive association is visible between total reviews and daily listens. however, the wide scatter indicates that review volume alone explains only a small proportion of variation in listening levels

Daily listens vs subscribers (by genre)

ggplot(podcasts_filtered, aes(x = subscribers, y = daily.listens, colour = genre)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Daily Listens vs Subscribers by Genre",
    x = "Subscribers",
    y = "Average Daily Listens",
    colour = "Genre")

Interpretation

A clear positive association is observed between subscribers and daily listens. Differences in both baseline levels and fitted slopes across genres motivate a subscribers × genre interaction model

Together, all these distributions appear realistic and appropriate for linear modelling

Model 1: Daily.listens ~ Review.score + Total.reviews

A multiple linear regression model was fitted to test whether review score and total reviews explain variation in average daily listens

Listen_reviews_main <- lm(
  daily.listens ~ review.score + total.reviews,
  data = podcasts_filtered)

summary(Listen_reviews_main)

Call:
lm(formula = daily.listens ~ review.score + total.reviews, data = podcasts_filtered)

Interpretation

NHST: Overall model test

H₀: Review score and total reviews do not explain variation in daily listens

H₁: At least one predictor is associated with daily listens

The model was statistically significant, F(2, 5350) = 86.75, p < .001, providing evidence against H₀.

Model fit

The model explained a small proportion of variation in daily listens (R² = 0.03141, adjusted R² = 0.03105), indicating limited explanatory power using review metrics alone.

Key estimates (estimation approach)

Review score was not associated with daily listens (β = −2.454, 95% CI [−13.687, 8.779], p = .669). Total reviews showed a clear positive association: each additional review was associated with 0.212 more daily listens (β = 0.212, 95% CI [0.181, 0.244], p < .001).

Conclusion

In this dataset, total review volume is associated with higher listens, but review score itself is not, and review metrics explain very little overall variation in daily listening levels

The model was statistically significant, F(4, 5348) = 2350, p < .001

Model fit

Including genre substantially increased explained variance (R² = 0.6373; adjusted R² = 0.6371), indicating that genre accounts for a large share of variation in daily listens beyond review metrics

Key estimates (estimation approach)

After controlling for review score and total reviews, Documentary podcasts received substantially fewer daily listens than Comedy (β = −367.863, 95% CI [−375.500, −360.226], p < .001), and News & Culture podcasts also received fewer daily listens than Comedy (β = −190.871, 95% CI [−198.462, −183.281], p < .001). Total reviews remained positively associated with listens (β = 0.331, 95% CI [0.312, 0.351], p < .001), while review score was not associated (β = −1.006, 95% CI [−7.882, 5.868], p = .774)

Conclusion

Genre is the dominant determinant of daily listens, while total reviews adds a smaller but statistically clear association; review score adds no evidence of additional explanatory value once the other variables are included

Model 4: Daily.Listens ~ Subscribers * Genre & Anova Test

An interaction model was fitted to test whether the association between subscribers and daily listens differs by genre. Moreover, an ANOVA was used to test whether including a Subscribers × Genre interaction significantly improves model fit over the additive model

  data = podcasts_filtered)

  Res.Df      RSS Df Sum of Sq      F    Pr(>F)    
1   5349 76109111                                  
2   5347 75835971  2    273141 9.6292 6.693e-05 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Interpretation

NHST: Interaction test

H₀: The association between subscribers and daily listens does not differ by genre H₁: The association differs by genre

The ANOVA comparison showed the interaction model improved fit relative to the additive model, F(2, 5347) = 9.63, p = 6.69×10⁻⁵

Model fit

The interaction model explained slightly more variance (R² = 0.6132; adjusted R² = 0.6128) than the additive model, indicating a small but statistically reliable improvement.

Key estimates (estimation approach)

For the reference genre (Comedy), each additional subscriber was associated with 0.326 more daily listens (β = 0.3258, 95% CI [0.282, 0.369], p < .001). The Subscribers × Documentary interaction was negative and statistically significant (β = −0.0790, 95% CI [−0.140, −0.018], p = .0116), indicating that subscriber gains translate into smaller listening increases for Documentary podcasts than for Comedy. The Subscribers × News & Culture interaction was positive but not statistically significant at the 5% level (β = 0.0531, 95% CI [−0.0066, 0.1127], p = .081)

Conclusion

Because the interaction improves fit and directly answers whether subscriber effects differ by genre, Model 4 is preferred for inference about genre-specific subscriber effects. However, the improvement in explained variance over Model 3 is small, so Model 3 remains a reasonable simpler summary model if the goal is parsimony rather than interaction interpretation.

Estimated Subscriber Effects by Genre (emtrends)

Estimated marginal trends were computed to examine whether the association between subscribers and daily listens differs across podcast genres

emtrends(Listen_subs_interact, ~ genre, var = "subscribers")
 genre          subscribers.trend     SE   df lower.CL upper.CL
 Comedy                     0.326 0.0223 5347    0.282    0.369
 Documentary                0.247 0.0219 5347    0.204    0.290
 News & Culture             0.379 0.0207 5347    0.338    0.419

Confidence level used: 0.95

Interpretation

Estimated trends quantify the expected change in daily listens per additional subscriber for each genre. The expected increase is 0.326 for Comedy (95% CI [0.282, 0.369]), 0.247 for Documentary (95% CI [0.204, 0.290]), and 0.379 for News & Culture (95% CI [0.338, 0.419]). This directly supports the interaction result that subscriber growth translates into smaller listening gains for Documentary podcasts than for Comedy.

Diagnostics

Model diagnostics were examined to assess whether the assumptions of linear regression were reasonably satisfied

par(mfrow=c(2,2), mar=c(4,4,2,1))
plot(Listen_reviews_genre)

par(mfrow=c(1,1))

par(mfrow=c(2,2), mar=c(4,4,2,1))
plot(Listen_subs_interact)

par(mfrow=c(1,1))

Interpretation

Diagnostics: Listen_reviews_genre

Diagnostic plots showed no major violations of linear regression assumptions. Residuals were approximately normally distributed, with no strong evidence of heteroscedasticity or influential observations, supporting the validity of model inference.

Diagnostics: Listen_subs_interact

Diagnostic plots indicated that linearity and normality assumptions were reasonably satisfied. Residual variance was broadly constant across fitted values, and no influential observations were detected, supporting reliable interpretation of the interaction effects.

Therefore, There was also no indication of problematic multicollinearity, as coefficient estimates were stable and standard errors were reasonable across models

Final Conclusion

Review score and total reviews explain only a small proportion of variation in daily listens (R² ≈ 0.03). In contrast, subscriber count and genre explain a substantial share of listening differences across podcasts (R² ≈ 0.61–0.63). Subscriber growth is positively associated with daily listens across all genres, but this association is significantly weaker for Documentary podcasts than for Comedy. Overall, podcast popularity is driven primarily by audience size and genre rather than review-based metrics.
